difficultyReason: Two-step causal chain (policy → reduced emissions → improved air quality) where the weakener attacks the move from evidence to conclusion rather than either step in isolation. One distractor strengthens; another is accurate but out-of-scope.
stimulus: A regional environmental agency reported that since the city of Morrow introduced a congestion-pricing program three years ago, vehicle traffic in the city center has declined by 22 percent. Because vehicle exhaust is the primary source of airborne particulate matter in urban areas, the agency concluded that Morrow's downtown air quality has substantially improved since the program was implemented.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: During the three years since the congestion-pricing program began, a large construction project has filled Morrow's city center with dust and diesel-powered machinery.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Several neighboring cities that implemented similar congestion-pricing programs have reported measurable improvements in their downtown air quality.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Morrow's congestion-pricing program generates revenue that the city has used to expand its public transit network.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vehicles that remain in Morrow's city center after the pricing program was introduced tend to be older and less fuel-efficient than the average vehicle that was diverted away.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The agency's measurement of particulate matter relies on sensors placed at fixed monitoring stations throughout the city center.

explanations.correct: The argument's conclusion depends on the chain: less traffic → less vehicle exhaust → better air quality. Choice A introduces an alternative source of airborne particulate matter — construction dust and diesel machinery — that has been operating concurrently with the traffic reduction. Even if vehicle exhaust fell, this new major source of particulates undermines the conclusion that air quality has substantially improved, directly attacking the move from reduced traffic to improved air quality.
explanations.A: Correct. Introduces an alternative explanation — a major concurrent source of particulate pollution — that severs the link between reduced vehicle traffic and the predicted air-quality improvement.
explanations.B: Opposite-answer trap. Evidence that comparable programs improved air quality elsewhere actually strengthens the agency's conclusion by providing analogous support for the causal chain.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant. Expanding public transit is a downstream benefit of the pricing revenue, but it says nothing about whether air quality in the city center has in fact improved. Out-of-scope.
explanations.D: Too narrow / premise attack. This challenges whether the 22% traffic reduction actually reduced total emissions proportionally, but the effect is mild and indirect; the argument can still stand if even the older remaining vehicles emit less exhaust in aggregate than the 22% more vehicles did. Choice A more directly and completely undermines the conclusion.
explanations.E: Shift in subject. This raises a methodological quibble about measurement accuracy but does not establish that air quality failed to improve — only that measurement method is fixed-location. It does not introduce an alternative explanation or attack the premise-to-conclusion move substantively.
